summary:
Visitors to South Australia stand under the national framework: the federal Sex Discrimination Act has treated gender identity as a protected ground since 2013, and in August 2024 the Federal Court held in Tickle v Giggle that the protection extends to trans women as women, awarding compensation against a female-only dating app that had excluded a trans woman member. The precedent binds service providers nationally, including in South Australia.

State law supplies a parallel remedy. The Equal Opportunity Act 1984 was amended in 2016 to protect gender identity and sexual orientation, so discrimination on that ground is actionable under South Australian statute as well as federal statute.

Identity documents are the clearest visitor-facing advantage. Since 23 May 2017, under the Births, Deaths and Marriages Registration (Gender Identity) Amendment Act 2016, a South Australian can change the sex descriptor on a birth certificate with appropriate clinical treatment, with no sex-reassignment surgery required and no forced divorce if married. Non-binary and 'indeterminate' descriptors are available on state birth certificates. With the Australian Capital Territory, South Australia was one of the first two jurisdictions in the country to permit change without surgery.

Violence against trans people is addressed by two specific provisions. Hate-crime sentencing laws that explicitly cover sexual orientation, gender identity and intersex characteristics passed and were implemented in November 2021. The gay-panic defence was abolished on 1 December 2020 and took effect 1 April 2021, removing a mitigation argument that had been available to defendants who killed gay and, by extension, gender-nonconforming victims.

Conversion Practices Prohibition Act 2024 passed in October 2024 and has been in legal effect since 1 April 2025, so conversion practices are prohibited rather than merely discouraged.

There is no restrictive machinery aimed at trans visitors. No South Australian law confines bathrooms or changing facilities by gender identity, no border friction has been reported for trans travellers, and relationship recognition is settled: registered domestic relationships date from 1 August 2017 and same-sex marriage has been legal nationally since December 2017, which matters to couples arriving together.
tangentialFactors:
The protective pattern is national rather than isolated. Queensland strengthened discrimination and vilification protections for gender-diverse people in April 2024, and New South Wales passed the Equality Legislation Amendment (LGBTIQA+) Act 2024, so a visitor moving between Australian states encounters a broadly aligned regime.

Counterweights are documented at the national level. The Tickle v Giggle case itself grew out of organised exclusionary activism, and ANROWS research maps current and emerging threats to trans and gender diverse rights in Australia, naming organised exclusionary campaigns, disputes over access to facilities and to records, and pressure to roll back existing rights. The same research documents systemic discrimination and harassment experienced by trans people, which is the lived backdrop to the statutory protections.

Detention is the sharpest residual risk in the country, and the sourced standards are Queensland's. Queensland's 2009 corrective services procedure on transgender prisoners was assessed as largely ineffective; oversight passed to the Inspector of Detention Services Act 2022, fully in force from 2023, and inspection standards issued in August 2023 for Queensland prisons and youth detention centres direct that transgender and intersex prisoners are generally admitted to facilities corresponding to their lived or experienced gender, with a discretionary admission caveat and an exception tied to sexual reassignment surgery. South Australia has no equivalent sourced placement rule in this record.
localsOnly:
South Australia was the first Australian jurisdiction to decriminalise male homosexual activity, the law commencing 2 October 1975, and it remains the only jurisdiction whose scheme for historical gay convictions is 'spent' rather than expunged, under the Spent Convictions (Decriminalised Offences) Amendment Act 2013, in force 22 December 2013.

Same-sex couples have been able to adopt since 17 February 2017. The 2017 national postal survey returned 62.5% 'Yes' in South Australia.
outOfScopeNotes:
The record carries no South Australian incident series, complaint data or enforcement pattern for gender-identity discrimination, so the strength of enforcement behind the Equal Opportunity Act 1984 provisions is unresolved rather than established.

No South Australian policy on the placement of transgender prisoners, on strip-searching, or on housing by gender identity is sourced here; the only detention standards in the inventory are Queensland's and are reported as comparison, not as South Australian law.

Rules for changing gender markers on a South Australian driver licence, on the federal passport, and on Medicare or tax records are not sourced; only the state birth-certificate route is documented. Access to gender-affirming healthcare, waiting times and any gatekeeping requirements for visitors or residents are likewise not sourced.

One inventory item, a Queensland Human Rights Commission news item on discrimination protections, was not retrievable (HTTP 403) and is cited only as a different-state reform; its content is not independently verified here.
